articles.text: The Piedmont Scout Tree Lot is seeing record popularity this year. With only 60 trees not yet sold as of December 7, the Scouts have arranged for delivery of 300 more trees in time for this weekend. The new shipment includes 200 Douglas Firs of 6-7 feet and 100 Noble Firs of 5-6 feet. All trees are due to arrive by Friday, to meet customers’ needs through the weekend and into the following week. The initial shipment of 1,450 trees arrived the day after Thanksgiving but was missing 150 Silvertips of the 300 ordered due to drought and fire. Silvertips availability has been limited statewide this year. December 7 marks the earliest date the Piedmont Scout Tree Lot has been on the verge of selling out. It is the first time in the 53-year history of the tree lot that a supplemental shipment was ordered. “We’ve ordered more Noble and Douglas fir trees, but they won’t last long. So come one, come all, and get ‘em fresh from the farm, or delivered right to your door,” said volunteer David Ashton, who orders the trees. The Scouts got a head start this year with 250 trees preordered online prior to the opening day. Online sales have ended, but families can enjoy the popular tradition of going to the lot and having Scouts help pick out the perfect tree. Tree deliveries are still available. Overall, 19% of all trees sold were made online for delivery, 59% were purchased in person and 22 % of the tree were purchased online for pickup. “The most fun I have is seeing families with small children come out to pick a tree,” noted Tree Lot chair Tom Smegal. “One mom with a baby said it was her family tradition to take the ‘fresh cut’ disc and make it into an ornament in honor of each year’s tree. Obviously you can’t do that online.”

articles.text: The annual tree lighting ceremony officially kicked off the holiday season in Piedmont on December 1. The in-person event drew a larger crowd than normal in front of the Community Hall. The Piedmont Beautification Foundation (PBF) has hosted the annual tree lighting ceremony on the first Wednesday evening in December for over 50 years. PBF members maintain, install, and remove the festive LED lights that don the large Redwood tree in Piedmont Park. With the help of Public Works employees and Piedmont Garden Club members, the PBF completed their 57th year of the decorating task on November 30. The festivities on the evening of December 1 included caroling by the Piedmont High School Troubadours, candy cane distribution from young volunteers, and even a visit from Santa Claus. Children were invited to write letters to Santa and deposit them in a special mailbox addressed to the North Pole. Despite the busyness surrounding the holiday season, Santa Claus confirmed that he reads every letter. “I received so many letters last year from the children in Piedmont. articles.text: As an alumna of Piedmont schools and now a parent of a Havens 1st grader, I wanted to share why I support the Giving Campaign and ask others to join me. I attended Piedmont schools from K-12. Now, as I walk my daughter to school, I am reminded of my special experience growing up in Piedmont. I remember kindergarten at Wildwood and walking to school every day where beloved teachers Mrs. Weidkamp and Mrs. Schoenberg introduced us to classroom learning. As a first grader, I sang “On the Sunny Side” every day with Mrs. Morrison. In high school, I perfected my bird-calling skills (and yes – my claim to fame – my Wildwood friend and I won the bird-calling contest and performed on the David Letterman show). I was lucky to have fabulous, amazing, wonderful teachers – many of whom I am still in touch with today, decades later. From small class sizes and aides in elementary school, to library time and electives in middle school, to AP classes in high school, I greatly benefited from the generosity of our community. Fast forward 20 years. My husband and I are living in Piedmont with our three children. This fall, our daughter, Lily, started at Havens as a first grader. We started off this school year nervously – how would our daughter adjust to first grade? Would Havens live up to the memories and expectations I had of Piedmont schools? We were thrilled to see that from her very first day, Lily was over the moon at Havens. Principal Dolid, Mrs. Fredericks, and the resource specialists have made this a smooth and wonderful experience. Lily is confident, she is engaged, and she simply loves school. We feel a great sense of comfort and peace in knowing that our kids will have an amazing public school experience here in Piedmont. Piedmont schools deserve our very best to ensure our young ones can continue to develop, thrive, and grow. We hope you’ll join us in supporting Piedmont Schools through the Piedmont Giving Campaign this year.
articles.title: Full circle with Piedmont schools

articles.text: The holiday season is a time for gathering, showing one another love and warmth, and thinking about resolutions for the new year. This season also provides opportunities to reduce waste, emissions, and our climate footprints throughout the holidays. From the gifts we give, to the ways we wrap those gifts, decorate, travel, and even the food we eat, our decisions make an impact on the world around us. If you’re searching the internet for ethical, eco-friendly holiday ideas, a simple google search will give you many ideas. However, the Piedmont Sustainability Team has compiled some tips and tricks for greening the holiday season. While the winter holiday season brings many of us good cheer, it also contributes more solid waste to landfills, harm to the environment, and emissions to our carbon footprint. Each year, Americans throw away approximately 25% more trash during the Thanksgiving to New Year’s holiday period than any other time of the year. This contributes an extra 25 million tons of garbage nationally, about 1 million extra tons per week. When thinking about how to reduce your climate footprint this holiday season, consider the three Rs: reduce, reuse, recycle. • Reduce From gift giving to wrapping to decorations, we often purchase single-use materials and contribute to unnecessary greenhouse gas emissions. One way to reduce your greater carbon footprint is by shopping locally. Shopping locally reduces the transportation emissions of goods and the overall carbon footprint of the product. Local shopping guides like those from Visit Oakland and Berkeley Holidays offer a wide range of ideas close to home for all audiences and price points. Other options to reduce gift-related waste are some clutter-free gift ideas including experiences, classes, memberships, and consumables. • Reuse Another way to reduce your carbon footprint this holiday season is through gifting secondhand items. Local thrift, vintage, and antique stores give products a second life, keeping them out of landfills and reducing emissions associated with the creation of new products and the transportation of said products. Not only do thrift, vintage, and antique stores decrease the carbon footprint of your gifts, but they also often contribute to local charities, boosting local community development. Gifting durable, reusable items and necessities will also ensure that your gift is used and lasts the test of time. Re-gifting is another sustainable option, especially for events like white elephant gift exchanges when the gift is not personalized and could be for someone you don’t know well. • Recycle Purchasing recycled-content products, or products contained in recyclable packaging materials decreases the waste that enters landfills. When wrapping gifts, consider recycling wrapping paper, reusing wrapping fabrics or bags and items such as ribbons and bows, or making your own from magazines, maps, or newspapers, such as an old edition of the Piedmont Post. If it’s necessary to purchase new wrapping paper, look for products that are recyclable and made from recycled materials. In some cultures, like the Japanese tradition of furoshiki, gifts are wrapped in cloth. Some potential cloth wrapping materials include tea towels or scarves, which make the wrapping cloth part of the gift itself. Better yet, give a gift that requires no packaging like an experience, class, membership, or donation in someone’s honor. Other opportunities for greening the holiday season this winter include turning off holiday lights during the day and when you go to bed, donating edible food, composting food scraps and your Christmas tree, minimizing personal vehicle use, and serving meals to your guests using reusable foodware when entertaining. Further editions of the Climate Corner will focus on additional opportunities to reduce your climate footprint and green the holidays this year. articles.text: The Piedmont Post returned to Piedmont High to report from inside classrooms after a 20-month hiatus due to Covid safety measures. Equipped with a mask and with vaccination card, school approval and health screener results in hand, this reporter visited the new STEAM building to see what Marna Chamberlain’s College Preparatory Physics class was working on. On Thursday December 2, Chamberlain’s period four Physics class continued building and refining solar ovens in groups of two. The immediate goal was to design and create a solar oven capable of heating up something edible. The overarching aim was to try to create solutions to the issue of inequity, locally and globally, regarding access to energy. Drawing her students’ attention to the bigger picture, she said, “Remember, we are addressA solar oven on the Makers Lab patio heats up some s’mores. PHS Physics Teacher Marna Chamberlain reviews 11th grader Audrey Harmon’s solar oven project. ing equity and finding solutions that are sustainable and realistic for their given target population.” No stranger to the project, Chamberlain had students building and donating them to Native Americans in 2014, and later arranged for students to build solar panels with a USB charging port and to be sent to Uganda and Haiti. “Our design could be used locally by kids as a fun project. Moms might have these basic supplies like cotton balls, shoeboxes, and construction paper around the house,” added student Eva Levingston. The amenities of the new science lab were at their disposal, and ingenuity, problem-solving and innovation were on display. Miter saws, razor blades, drills, hot glue guns were the tools, and cardboard, plywood, tin foil, saran wrap, spray paint and plexiglass were the favored supplies. Some students used shoe boxes as their base, others modified pizza boxes and some ovens resembled wooden bird houses. Students were given free rein to choose their own design without many constraints so there was considerable variety between groups. Many students had the goal of making water safe for consumption. But with only an hour of time to have the ovens out in the winter sun, many opted instead to make s’mores or Rice Krispies treats. Students were directed to research the dual properties of light, both as a particle and as a wave, and to use that knowledge in conjunction with the material science of the building supplies. Senior Ana Romanczuk and Junior Milani Juarbe explained their design. “We have aluminum foil so we can reflect the light through saran wrap. Everything inside will be black, so the heat will get attracted to it, and it will end up getting trapped inside.” Students also learned about the Angle of Isolation – choosing the best angle to position the light reflecting material of the ovens, like tin foil or mirrors. Chamberlain explained the importance of recording accurate data and following the scientific method even if designs and tests don’t work out as planned “Sometimes, efficiency goes down after attempting improvements, and that is okay. Even in something like rocketry, the first model may perform the best,” she said. From March 2020 to March 2021 all classes at PHS were taught remotely on computers because of the Covid pandemic. Now that school has been back in person full-time since August, students in classes like Physics have the chance to experience the full process of creation and experimentation. With the new STEAM building on the high school campus, Piedmont students have the latest in technology to advance their studies. Perseas Gioukaris (left) and Eva Levingston hold up their solar oven, which has feet on the bottom to limit heat transfer. Kevin Blodgett (left) and Harry Pasion test their solar oven by recording the temperature inside with an aquarium thermometer.

articles.text: As the weather gets colder and more drizzly, I find it good to curl up with my tuxedo cat, a fluffy duvet, and a nice cup of tea. To round it out, I love a good mystery. Mysteries come in all flavors. I joined a Mystery Book Club for several years at my local library, enabling me to expand my usual stable of mystery authors. I enjoy books featuring forensic investigators, smart female detectives, England, especially during the Victorian period, and ethical dilemmas. Most of the books are light on graphic violence. Here are a variety of choices, all of which I have read. Enola Holmes Mystery Series by Nancy Springer. Philomel Books. 2006. The Case of the Missing Marquess. 236 pages. This would be a good series for a family read. I enjoyed her character as an adult and I can see middle schoolers also enjoying her adventures. Her first story, The Case of the Missing Marquess has been made into a movie on Netflix. The setting is the English countryside and Victorian London. Enola is the teenaged sister of Sherlock and Mycroft Holmes. She is eccentric and high spirited, solving her own mysteries, while her brothers try to keep her from getting into too much trouble. She is generally a few steps ahead of them. She is also a master (mistress?) of disguise. voices. Anyone who has visited or attended Harvard will recognize many of the landmarks. The House on Vesper Sands was named an Indie Next Pick, Library Reads Pick, Apple Books’ Best Book, Powells’ Pick, Amazon Fiction & Literature’s “Best of the Month,” and one of Daily’s Best Historical Novels of 2021. An Anonymous Girl by Greer Hendricks & Sarah Pekkanen. St. Martin’s Group Publishing. 2019. 375 pages. A young woman joins a psychological study at the local university, drawn by the opportunity to make some much needed money. articles.text: 11th annual girls’ basketball tournament at PHS After a one-year hiatus due to the global pandemic, the Paris Twins Classic returns to Binks Rawlings Gym this week from Thursday through Saturday, December 9-11. It is the 11th year of the annual tournament named for Sports Hall of Fame athletes Courtney and Ashley Paris, who led Piedmont to two consecutive state championships. “Our tournament is going to be thick with competition. We’ve only won this one time, and it’ll be tough to do it again. We’re excited,” said coach Bryan Gardere. Piedmont will face Lompoc in the opening game tomorrow, Thursday, December 9 at 8:00 p.m. Piedmont recently beat Lompoc 74-40 on December 2 at the Lompoc tournament. The Highlanders won the tournament after being a finalist last year. Also competing on the opening day at 3:30 p.m. will be Cardinal Newman, which holds a 4-2 overall record and had a 29-4 record last year. It plays Grant Union from Sacramento. a team with a 6-1 record. Piedmont will play the winner of that game on Friday, December 10 at 6:30 p.m. Game 2 is slated for 5:00 p.m. tomorrow with Vanden of Fairfield (2-0) playing Sacred Heart (2-1). Vanden recently beat Pleasant Valley 73-35 and Chico 72-39. “Vanden is another tough school; they made it to the second-round of the State Tournament [in the winter of 2020]. It’s a really deep tournament,” said Gardere. Game 3 is at 6:30 p.m., featuring Freedom HS Oakley (2-1) against Valley Christian of San Jose (4-0). The winners of Vanden vs. Sacred Heart will face the winner of Freedom vs. Valley Christian on Friday at 8:00 p.m. The Championship game is scheduled for Saturday, December 11 at 2:30 p.m. with a 3rd place game at 1:00 p.m.

articles.text: The Piedmont girls’ basketball team started its season in a big way. Playing 300 miles from home in Lompoc, they won the annual Bryan Ayer Classic for the second time in three years. On Thursday, December 2, they rolled over Santa Barbara, 57-34; trounced host Lompoc on Friday 74-40, and won the finals 62-34 over Orcutt Academy. It marked the 14th annual tournament following last spring’s pandemic shortened season. In 2019, PHS lost to Santa Barbara in the championship 64-54. Sophomore Natalia Martinez was named MVP of the tournament, and juniors Trinity Zamora and Maddie Hill were named to the All-Tournament team. “I am proud of our whole team. We aren’t close to the final product, but definitely off to solid start,” said coach Bryan Gardere. “We can build from this weekend. Trinity [Zamora], Natalia [Martinez], Maddie [Hill] and Hannah [Govert] led the way. Kat Melian truly stepped up in her first action on varsity. I’m so proud of her,” Finals vs. Orcutt Academy Piedmont led 18-7 at the end of the first quarter and ballooned to 39-17 by halftime. It was after three quarters before finishing with a 62-34 victory for the championship. In the first quarter, Piedmont made five three-pointers, two each by Zamora and Hill, and one by Hannah Govert. Martinez exploded for 13 of her 27 points Natalia Martinez was named the tournament’s Most Outstanding Player. I the second quarter, including 4 for 5 at the free throw line. Martinez added 10 more points in the third quarter including 4 of 4 at the line. Hill had a 3-pointer, and Shay Ottaviano scored her first varsity field goal. Final stats include Martinez with 27 points, six rebounds, two assists, and five steals. Zamora scored 16 points, eight rebounds, eight assists, three steals, and two blocks. Hill came away with 12 points, two rebounds, three assists, and two steals. Govert scored three points, seven rebounds, four assists, and two blocks. Melian had five rebounds, two steals. articles.text: Piedmont’s boys’ basketball team hosted its Holiday Tournament from Thursday through Saturday, December 2-4. It marked the return of Piedmont’s early-December tourney, formerly sponsored by the Otis Spunkmeyer Cookie company, to help welcome the start of the season. The tradition started more than 15 years ago by former coach Chris Lavdiotis. “Hosting a tournament means so many things on many different levels,” noted coach Ben Spencer. “We’re getting back to normal, it means our athletic department can build funding again, and most importantly, our kids can compete at a high level against some of the best teams in the Bay Area. The Piedmont Holiday Tournament (formerly the Otis Spunkmeyer Invitational) has been a great tradition for our program. It means that the basketball season is officially here,” The Highlanders lost in the finals against Northgate 56-42 on Saturday. PHS defeated Freedom 56-47 in the semifinals on Friday after opening with a 67-40 win over Terra Linda on Thursday. Piedmont was moved up from Div. 4 to Div. 3 (larger enrollment schools in North Coast Section) after last year’s highly successful season. None of the games came against divisional opponents; Northgate is Div. 2, Freedom is Div. 1, and Terra Linda remained a Div. 4 team. The Highlanders defeated Northgate 88-82 in the spring of 2021, so the Broncos were back looking for a little payback. “I thought Northgate came ready to play knowing that we beat them last year. They came out with a lot of energy and did well defending our two key players. Our defense is a bit ahead of our offense, which will pay larger dividends later in the season,” said assistant coach Shamaree Worley. “We have to keep working on the offense and getting more people to contribute as scorers to take the load off of A.J. and JoJo.” A.J. Harris led the way in the finals with 16 points against Northgate. He had 19 points against Freedom, and 21 against Terra Linda. JoJo Murphy opened with 24 points against Terra Linda, followed by 20 points against Freedom. He tweaked his ankle toward the end of the semifinals and played through pain to score eight points I the finals. The PHS student section showed up in numbers for the PHS Holiday Tournament. Staff Photos Piedmont’s boys’ basketball team hosted its Holiday Tournament, falling in the finals to Northgate 56-42. Finals vs. Northgate Northgate opened with a 17-8 lead, and Piedmont trailed 30-24 at the half. PHS struggled in the third with just three points, falling behind 42-27 by the start of the fourth, closing out 56-42. The Broncos started strong by building a 13-3 lead before Bautista Costa knocked down a 3-pointer, following by Harris scoring to narrow the deficit as Murphy sat on the bench. Murphy entered in the second period and made a visible impact as space on the floor opened. Harris had eight points in the quarter with two 3-pointers, while Murphy had four. Harris opened the second half with a 3-pointer after a steal, but that was all Piedmont would be able to do. Northgate’s defenders made three blocks and had a pair of steals during a 17-0 scoring run stretching into the fourth quarter. PHS did well to put up 15 points and narrow the deficit to 49-36 in the final period. Murphy had four and Harris had three in the fourth quarter. Final stats: Harris with 16 points, Murphy had eight, Spencer Settlemier had six points, Raydan Holmes had five. Semifinals vs. Freedom Piedmont opened with a 15-7 lead in the first quarter and went up 31-16 by halftime. The Highlanders went into the fourth with a 47-33 lead and closed out strong 56-47. Murphy opened strong in the first quarter with seven points including a 3-pointer. Another strong defensive quarter in the second helped PHS keep a 15-point advantage by halftime. Murphy put in six points and Harris scored seven points, Coach Ben Spencer sends in guard Matthew Riordan. A.J. Harris scored 16 points against Northgate, 19 points against Freedom, and 21 against Terra Linda. articles.text: Christmas Revels will present its 36th season of holiday events with performances of “La Sirène” at the First Congregational Church of Oakland from December 11-19. This year’s show features a full chorus, elaborate costumes, traditional music and dance, and a sea monster. California Revels dives into the Age of Sail, blending 19th Century London with folklore and traditions from the Caribbean and Gullah Islands in an odyssey across the Atlantic. From sea chanties, mermaids, and Christmas carols to Jonkonnu and Papa Bois, the performances will celebrate the Winter Solstice. Audiences of all ages will appreciate the glories of traditional music, dance, ritual and folk plays, including the mesmerizing “Antler Dance,” all with top Bay Area musicians, actors, and performers. La Sirène is directed by Amy Marie Haven and written by Jeff Raz. California Revels is led by Artistic Director Rene Collins and Music Director Shira Kammen. Anne Bingham Goess is Associate Music Director. Christopher Bryden is Children’s Music Director. Choreographed by Jeri Reed. Tickets are $15-$75. First Congregational Church of Oakland is located at 2501 Harrison Street in Oakland. All guests must be fully-vaccinated against COVID-19; a COVID-19 Safety Policy will be in effect. articles.text: Thanksgiving is a distant memory. Black Friday signals the race toward Christmas. Can it be coincidence that I am reminded of the mantra of the Indianapolis 500… “Start your engines.“ It is good to ask ourselves tough questions which can also be inspirational. For example… What does it take to be a concert performer? The nerves of a bull fighter, the grace of a ballerina. The enterprise of a politician, and the endurance of a marathon runner. It also helps to have the intelligence of Socrates, the artistic concept of Picasso, and don’t forget a little bit of the heart. Be sure to study nature in all of its variety. Try to play passages of music differently every time and still be musically correct in every way. Never pander to the audience. Be sincere and forthright. Always retain your dignity both personally and artistically. While you do this you must, at the same time, be flexible. All of these things were made crystal clear on Sunday when I was a judge at the Northern California Young Talents music competition in Livermore. Rimma Radayeva is the driving force. Her organization of the festival ran like clockwork. There was not one glitch for five straight hours. All of the students and their families live the inspiration of the American dream. Their diligence and hard work is exemplary. It was not that everyone played perfectly. What was important is that they played with diligence and inspiration. Holiday music was not neglected either this weekend. There was a beautifully staged production of “Scrooge…The Musical“ at the Mormon Temple Hill auditorium. This was a fully-staged production with a full symphony orchestra and impressive sets. The orchestra was conducted crisply by Matt Mackey, resulting in the orchestra playing in inspired fashion. I kept watching Mackey and I asked myself “who is this guy?” He is a really good conductor. I found out that he is the Band Director at Elk Grove High School outside Sacramento. Those kids are sure lucky. The rest of the production was first class. It is interesting to note that everyone on stage and behind stage is an amateur, but you’d never know it. Everything was of professional quality. The audience rose as one at the end to applaud – a standing ovation that was well deserved. And that’s just the tip of the iceberg… If you know where to look. The Church of Jesus Christ of Latter-day Saints’ Oakland California Temple is located in the Oakland Hills at 4766 Lincoln Avenue. Musicians Steve Oda, Michael Lewis and Pushpa Oda will perform a selection of North Indian classical music this Saturday, December 11, at Piedmont Center for the Arts beginning at 7 p.m. The music will be followed by a dance performance by Kali Futnani, a senior teacher at Bharata Kalanjali in Berkeley. Futnani began her dance training at Kalanjali in Berkeley, which was founded by K.P and Katherine Kunhiraman. She has a BFA from Kalakshetra College of Fine Arts in Chennai, India. Kali continued her training under K.P. Yesodha in Chennai for six years, performing with the company throughout India before returning to the Bay Area. Bharatanatyam is a South Indian classical dance style that was performed in the temples of Tamil Nadu for thousands of years before coming to the stage. Bharatanatyam has both rhythmic and dramatic aspects. The theory of rasa, the nature of the aesthetics as transcendental and emotional experience, is central to all Indian arts. Through movement set to rhythmic patterns and storytelling through hand gestures and expression, the audience and the performer have a shared experience through art. Tickets are $20 at the door, and $10 for students with high school or college identification. All events at Piedmont Center for the Arts require proof of vaccination and proper masking while indoors.

articles.text: Four East Bay artists will present an exhibition entitled A Boundless Moment at Piedmont Center for the Arts this Saturday and Sunday, December 11-12. Gallery hours are from 11 a.m. to 2 p.m. The exhibition will showcase the works of Carl Heyward, Akiko Suzuki, Usha Shukla, and Colleen Gianatiempo. Heyward is a NEA (National Endowment for the Arts) grant recipient and a former Masters of Fine Arts instructor at the San Francisco Academy of Art University. His work has been featured at various art galleries in the Bay Area and internationally. “Yarrow 03” oil on canvas, 36x36” by Usha Shukla Artist Usha Shukla Suzuki is a textile and mixed media artist based in San Francisco. Since 2014, she has participated in the Global Art Project with partner Heyward. “My work expresses the invisible nature of thought, of skin sensation, the poetry of Love and Eros or the presentiments that occur prior to thought. Intuitive works are born from everyday life as are novels,” Suzuki said. “The words borne out of the flood of my imagery become poetry and are visualized in works as abstractions through paint, collage, sewing and fiber works.” Shukla was born and raised in New Delhi, India; the vibrant colors of the Indian countryside greatly influence her artwork. She completed a graduate program at the Academy of Art University, San Francisco, with a focus on painting. She paints primarily large abstracts in vivid colors and has a unique process of “mark-making.” Gianatiempo is a mixed media artist, educator, and designer living in the East Bay. “My journey as an artist began when I was 3 years old. I remember cutting up family photos and drawing on walls with lipstick. I learned early on that it’s possible to express the world around me in different ways and this is where my passion began,” Gianatiempo said. “Nature is my main influence as I always marvel about the design and beauty it beholds,” she said. “I work in many mediums and thrive most when I can experiment and discover new techniques. I have been told that I am the Mary Poppins of art supplies! Proof of vaccination and masking indoors is required at all Piedmont Center for the Arts events. “Silent Majority” blue textile 63x56” by Akiko Suzuki

articles.text: Berkeley Symphony music series opens Dec. 12 in Piedmont Composer Jessie Montgomery The long-standing chamber music series with Berkeley Symphony musicians and friends continues this Sunday, December 12, with a concert at the Piedmont Center of the Arts at 4 p.m. Four extraordinary Berkeley Symphony string players will assemble for a dynamic exploration of classic and contemporary chamber music with a thrillingly improvisatory feel, culminating with Debussy’s iconic impressionist masterpiece. Violi nists Nigel A r mstrong and Emanuela Nikiforova will be joined by violist Ivo Bokulic and cellist Isaac Pastor-Chermak in a performance of Jessie Montgomery’s Voodoo Dolls for String Quartet, Brian Nabors’ Theme and Variations for solo violin, Winter from Four Seasons by Antonio Vivaldi, and Claude Debussy’s String Quartet in G minor. Tickets are $35 and are available online at berkeleysymphony. org, by calling Berkeley Symphony’s box office at 510-841-2800, ext. 1, or at the door. Piedmont Center for the Arts is located at 801 Magnolia Avenue. Proof of vaccination and photo ID is required. Nigel Armstrong, violin Nigel Armstrong is a dynamic and creative artist both within and beyond the realm of classical music. From his musical beginnings as a member of “The Little Fiddlers” in Sonoma, to collaborations with tango musicians in Argentina, he has enjoyed using the violin in a versatile manner throughout his life. As soloist Nigel has performed with orchestras such as the Dusseldorf Symphony, the Los Angeles Chamber Orchestra, the St. Petersburg Philharmonic, YOA Orchestra of the Americas, and the Boston Pops, and with conductors including Sir Neville Marriner and Carlos Miguel Prieto. He received the 2nd Prize, the Ole Bull Prize, and the Nordheim Award at the 2010 Menuhin Competition Senior Division in Oslo, Norway, and got the 4th Prize plus the Prize for the Best Performance of the Commissioned Work (STOMP, by John Corigliano) at the XIV International Tchaikovsky Competition. As a chamber musician his concerts have taken him across the US and abroad--highlights have included opportunities to share the stage with the Tokyo String Quartet and pianist Jonathan Biss. Since 2009 he has appeared as concertmaster with the Colburn Orchestra, LA’s American Youth Symphony, the Curtis Symphony Orchestra, YOA Orchestra of the Americas, and the New York String Orchestra in their annual Carnegie hall performances. Beginning in the 2016/17 season he serves as concertmaster of the Santa Cruz Symphony. A graduate of the Colburn School and the Curtis Institute of Music. He also recently had the opportunity to live with and learn from the Plum Village community founded by Buddhist monk Thich Nhat Hanh, where he spent a year. Emanuela Nikiforova, violin A native of Bulgaria, Emanuela Nikiforova benefited from the influence of the Russian violin school at Varna and Sofia middle and high music schools, and the influence of Yfrah Neaman and Neaman’s esteemed student, Professor Kevork Mardirossian (Louisiana State University School of Music). She is also influenced by Yehudi Menuhin and Argentinian Alberto Lysy at the International Menuhin Music Academy in Gstaad, Switzerland. And by Camilla Wicks at the San Francisco Conservatory of Music. Nikiforova has performed on three different continents from a young age as a soloist, chamber and orchestra musician. She is a former member of Camerata Lysy, Camerata Bariloche, Philharmonica de Buenos Aires, Sarasota Orchestra and Baton Rouge Symphony, and a current member of the Santa Rosa, Marin, Berkeley, Oakland and Silicon Valley symphonies, a substitute at the San Francisco Ballet, Opera San Jose, California and Napa symphonies and others. Nigel-Armstrong Ivo Bokulic Ivo Bokulic, viola Born in Croatia, raised in Chicago, and based in San Francisco, Ivo Bokulic is Associate Principal Violist of the San José Chamber Orchestra and also holds positions with Opera San José & Berkeley Symphony. An active freelance musician in the Bay Area and beyond, Ivo performs with groups such as the New Century Chamber Orchestra, Utah Festival Opera, Santa Rosa Symphony, San Francisco Chamber Orchestra, California Symphony, Reno Philharmonic, Marin Symphony, Oakland Symphony, Fresno Philharmonic, Modesto Symphony Orchestra, Santa Cruz Symphony, and One Found Sound. As a member of Isaac Pastor-Chermak San Francisco’s Magik*Magik Orchestra, Ivo has toured, recorded, and performed with acts such as Death Cab for Cutie, Sting, Father John Misty, Gregory Porter, and Third Eye Blind. He holds both Bachelor and Master of Music degrees from the San Francisco Conservatory of Music, where he studied with Jodi Levitz. He plays a viola made in 1999 by Hiroshi Iizuka. Isaac Pastor-Chermak, cello Isaac Pastor-Chermak leads an active musical life as a cellist, teacher, conductor, and administrator. A career orchestral player, on any given weekend he can be found performing as Principal Cellist of the Waterloo-Cedar Falls Symphony; Associate Principal Cellist of the Stockton Symphony; Assistant Principal Cellist of Opera San Jose and Fresno Philharmonic; and a member of the Berkeley Symphony, Monterey Symphony, Santa Cruz Symphony, Santa Barbara Symphony, and Dayton Philharmonic. He fills his summers with teaching and chamber music projects. In addition, he is Assistant Principal Cellist at the Eisenstadt Classical Music Festival in Austria, and Co-Principal Cellist of the Lake Tahoe Music Festival. In past seasons, he has enjoyed time as Principal Cellist of Portland Opera, as well as membership in the West Virginia Symphony and Walla Walla Symphony. He maintains a wide range of chamber music commitments with favorite colleagues. He is the cellist of Black Cedar Trio, the only flute-cello-guitar ensemble in the United States. articles.text: Visit Filoli Historic House & Garden in Woodside throughout the month to see the 16-acre estate in all its festive glory. The non-profit, registered landmark, will be celebrating “Holidays at Filoli” through January 2. The impressive myriad of decorations that were installed last month enhances the estate’s historic and renowned elegance. Filoli has a designated holiday decor team responsible for installing over a dozen decorated trees inside and outside the mansion, and miles upon miles of twinkling lights in all colors that don the gardens and drape the interior. Walking through the 16-acre estate, you will find 22 festooned Christmas trees, 3,600 light strands that stretch more than 18 miles, over 7,000 luminescent ornaments, and 1,000 feet of festive garlands. The Reception Room’s 18-foot ceilings create an appropriate adobe for “The Grand Tree,” the tallest of those on display. The two-story mansion contains 56 rooms, including a large ballroom and reception room designed to host concerts and debut balls. Each room in the mansion is adorned with holiday decorations that complement the room’s original hues and aesthetics. The design team carefully recreate the original holiday placement that is indicative of Agnes and William Bourn, the house’s first residents. The Bourns decorated with natural materials from the gardens, including pinecones and evergreen wreaths. Realistic artificial trees and garlands were not yet available in early to mid-1900s. More original artifacts can be viewed throughout the home. Lurline Roth, who lived with her family in the mansion after the Bourns, was an avid collector of religious icons. Her Italian Murano glass nativity scene, one of her favorites, is displayed in the study. While holiday evenings at Filoli are truly a sight to see, the lighting enhancements glow just as brightly in daylight. Daytime admission gains you access to explore the estate trail before sundown and admire the garden’s autumnal colors. articles.text: Piedmont Seniors at the Oakland Zoo: (front) Mona Jamieson (left), Margaret Brownell, Janet Epstein, Greg Jurin, Yorkman Lowe, and Madeline Mooore; back row: Jim Ayotte, Irene Westler, Susan McCreary, and Sandra Curach. Not pictured: Havaleh Kapellas. The Piedmont Seniors ventured out on their second excursion since the COVID-19 shutdown to visit the nearby Oakland Zoo. The zoo was established in 1922, and is currently home to over 850 native and exotic animals. The zoo is recognized for its outstanding animal care, particularly its elephant care program. There is also a children’s petting zoo and when you explore the grounds, you will see chimpanzees, squirrel monkeys, a variety of birds, camels, giraffes, and more. If you haven’t been there in quite a while you are in for a big surprise. In 2018 the zoo expanded to form the California Trail. The best part was traveling in an aerial gondola from the existing zoo. The gondola ride continues at a slow pace at the entrances and exits. The view at the top is spectacular and one can see miles of the East and West Bay Areas! Once the members arrived after a 4 minute enclosed ride, the group saw black bears, American bison, eagles, gray wolves, coyotes, and even mountain lions. There is a pleasant lunch spot at the top, where one can order tasty food at the Landing Café. Again, the scenery is spectacular and such a great spot to enjoy a relaxing meal. The zoo website is “high-tech”, and it is easy to order lunch from their website. You simply select your food and choose the time when you want to pick it up. Should you choose to remain on the lower level, you can also use their website to order food at the Tuskers Grill. There is a terrific train ride that is available that goes all around the perimeter of the zoo, which gives a nice overview of what visitors will be seeing. pages.text: Wednesday, December 8, 2021 25 Piedmont Seniors enchanted with Oakland Zoo Piedmont Seniors at the Oakland Zoo: (front) Mona Jamieson (left), Margaret Brownell, Janet Epstein, Greg Jurin, Yorkman Lowe, and Madeline Mooore; back row: Jim Ayotte, Irene Westler, Susan McCreary, and Sandra Curach. Not pictured: Havaleh Kapellas. By Janet Epstein The Piedmont Seniors ventured out on their second excursion since the COVID-19 shutdown to visit the nearby Oakland Zoo. The zoo was established in 1922, and is currently home to over 850 native and exotic animals. The zoo is recognized for its outstanding animal care, particularly its elephant care program. There is also a children’s petting zoo and when you explore the grounds, you will see chimpanzees, squirrel monkeys, a variety of birds, camels, giraffes, and more. If you haven’t been there in quite a while you are in for a big surprise. In 2018 the zoo expanded to form the California Trail. The best part was traveling in an aerial gondola from the existing zoo. The gondola ride continues at a slow pace at the entrances and exits. The view at the top is spectacular and one can see miles of the East and West Bay Areas! Once the members arrived after a 4 minute enclosed ride, the group saw black bears, American bison, eagles, gray wolves, coyotes, and even mountain lions. There is a pleasant lunch spot at the top, where one can order tasty food at the Landing Café. Again, the scenery is spectacular and such a great spot to enjoy a relaxing meal. The zoo website is “high-tech”, and it is easy to order lunch from their website. You simply select your food and choose the time when you want to pick it up. Should you choose to remain on the lower level, you can also use their website to order food at the Tuskers Grill. pages.text: Wednesday, December 8, 2021 27 Photos by Sierra Nevada Photos Nearly 50 Scouts and parents from Troop 11 had a river rafting trip on the American River the weekend of September 18. Troop 11 Scouts enjoy rafting on American River By Elles Krieckhaus Piedmont Scouts in Troop 11 went rafting on the South Fork of the American River the weekend of September 18 not far outside Sacramento. About 50 Scouts left early Saturday morning and drove in carpools. After learning about boating and water safety, we got on the water and went down the river smiling. The weather was warm and the water was great when we were able to get out of the rafts and swim. We stopped about halfway down the stretch of river and our guides provided a delicious lunch for us. Campfires were not allowed due to the high fire danger, so we spent time learning knife and ax skills and playing cards by lantern light. As we went to bed, we observed the full moon had a bright ring around it and the clouds were moving in, a sign of rain. The Scouts sleeping in tents were happy they did when it started raining late that night. But those in the tarp shelters stayed mostly dry too, except for one of the parents. Jesus understood blessings as challenges that open us up to more profoundly rely on each other and inspire us to rebuild together. Perhaps we should allow our “comparative gratitude” to disturb us in a way that leads to action, rather than lull us into complacency. So if a blessing is something that draws us toward a new and larger vision, maybe we should be thankful, not only for what we have now, but also for the opportunity to create and build something more inclusive, more peaceful, more beautiful, that might be described as one nation under God. Perhaps this understanding of what a real blessing is will help us not be discouraged by chaos, but rather, inspire us to pick up our shovels, hammers and levels and begin to build a better future for all. Although Piedmont is small with a very limited number of public buildings, it is interesting to note that the tallest are given to education! Considering what we currently have against successful small city models, I think the town center could be improved in future development by the addition of the following: 1. A main plaza – not so big, but strategically located at ground zero in the city, functioning as the natural meeting place. 2. Some more commercial – small convenient venues that would increase activity and vitality. 3. Mixed use residential – just like commercial, increasing activity and vitality. 4. Enhanced urban design between different parts of center, including planting, hardscape, lighting and signage. 5. Subordination and reduction of cars. Will Adams is a Planner, Urban Designer and Architect, who has lived in Piedmont for 30 years. He can be reached through will@MakingDesignSense.com The Veterans’ Memorial Building and Police Station and the Ellen Driscoll Playhouse and Havens School both flank busy Mulberry’s with their own nicely designed secondary plazas. Note the landmark character of the radio antennae of the police station (the 21st century church spire?). Of special note is how well the (relatively) new Havens school relates to and complements the historic Ellen Driscoll Playhouse: this is certainly good architecture and urban design! These higher buildings provide more density and vitality to the core; they provide enclosure to the ground level “outdoor rooms”, and they act as landmarks in the community.
